A man of mass $100 \mathrm{~kg}$. is standing on a platform of mass $200 \mathrm{~kg}$. which is kept on a smooth ice surface. If the man starts moving on the platform with a speed $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}$ relative to the platform then calculate with what velocity relative to the ice the platform will recoil?

solution.text:
Consider the situation shown in figure.Suppose the man moves at a speed w towards right and the the platform recoils at a speed \(\mathrm{V}\) towards left, both relative to the ice. Hence, the speed of the man relative to the platform is
\(\mathrm{V}+\mathrm{w}\). By the question,
\(\mathrm{V}+\mathrm{w}=\mathrm{v}\), or \(\mathrm{w}=\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{V} \ldots\) (i)
Taking the platform and the man to be the system, there is no external horizontal force on the system. The linear momentum of the system remains constant. Initially both the man and the platform were at rest. Thus,
\(0=\mathrm{MV}-\underset{m v}{\operatorname{mor}} \mathrm{MV}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{V})[\mathrm{Using}(\mathrm{i})]\)
or, \(V=\frac{m v}{M+m}\)
Hence, the velocity relative to the ice is \(V=\frac{m v}{M+m}\).

question.text: A spring is compressed between two toy carts of mass $\mathrm{m}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{m}_{2}$. When the toy carts are released, the springs exert equal and opposite average forces for the same time on each toy cart. If $v_{1}$ and $\mathrm{v}_{2}$ are the velocities of the toy carts and there is no friction between the toy carts and the ground, then :

solution.text:
Applying law of conservation of linear momentum
$\mathrm{m}_{1} \mathrm{v}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2} \mathrm{v}_{2}=0$
$\frac{\mathrm{m}_{1}}{\mathrm{~m}_{2}}=-\frac{\mathrm{v}_{2}}{\mathrm{v}_{1}}$ or $\frac{\mathrm{v}_{1}}{\mathrm{v}_{2}}=-\frac{\mathrm{m}_{2}}{\mathrm{~m}_{1}}$

topics.title: Centre of mass of discrete particles

question.text: Two bodies of mass 1 kg and 3 kg have position vectors $\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+k$ and $-3 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ respectively. The magnitude of position vector of centre of mass of this system will be similar to the magnitude of vector :

solution.text:
Position of COM of a mass - system is given as,
$\vec{r}_{\mathrm{com}}=\frac{m_1 \vec{r}_1+m_2 \vec{r}_2}{m_1+m_2}=\frac{1(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+\hat{k})+3(-3 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}}{1+3}$
$=-2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$
$\left|\vec{r}_{c m}\right|=|-2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}|=\sqrt{(2)^2+(1)^2+(1)^2}=\sqrt{6}$
Only option (1) magnitude is
$\sqrt{1^2+(-2)^2+1^2}=\sqrt{6}$
So option (1) is correct.

question.text: An object of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> is projected with a velocity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>20</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> at an angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, to the horizontal. At the highest point of its path, the projectile explodes and breaks up into two fragments of masses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi><mo>.</mo></math> The fragments separate horizontally after the explosion, which releases internal energy such that the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>K</mi><mi>E</mi></math> of the system af the highest point is doubled. The separation between the two fragments when they reach the ground is

solution.text:
Given, m=5 kg,v=20 m s-1,θ=60°

Vertical component of velocity, vy=v sin 60°

=20×32=103 m s-1

Time taken to reach the highest point = Time taken to reach the ground from highest point.

t=v sin θg=vyg=1039.8=1.77 s

At the highest point, m splits up into two parts of masses m1=1 kg and m2=4 kg

If their velocities are v1 and v2 respectively, then applying the principle of conservation of linear momentum, we get

m1v1+m2v2=mv cos θ

v1+4v2=5×20×12  ∵    θ=60°

v1+4v2=5×10=50     ....i

Initial KE=12 m v cos θ2

=12×5×102=250 J

Final KE=2 (initial KE)=2×250=500 J

∴  12m1v12+12m2v22=500

or   12×1×v12+12×4×v22=500

or   v12+4v22=1000     ....ii

Solving Eq. (i) and (ii), we get

v1=30 m s-1, v2=5 m s-1

Hence, the separation between the two fragments

=v1-v2×t=30-5×1.77 m=44.25 m

question.text: A system consists of three particles, each of mass $\mathrm{m}$ and located at (1,1),(2,2) and (3,3) . The co-ordinates of the centre of mass are

solution.text:
The coordinates of C.M of three particle are
\begin{array}{c}
\mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_{1} \mathrm{x}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2} \mathrm{x}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3} \mathrm{x}_{3}}{\mathrm{~m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3}} \& \mathrm{y}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_{1} \mathrm{y}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2} \mathrm{y}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3} \mathrm{y}_{3}}{\mathrm{~m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3}} \\
\text { here } \mathrm{m}_{1}=\mathrm{m}_{2}=\mathrm{m}_{3}=\mathrm{m} \\
\text { so } \mathrm{x}=\frac{\left(\mathrm{x}_{1}+\mathrm{x}_{2}+\mathrm{x}_{3}\right) \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}}=2
\end{array}
$$
y=\frac{\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right) m}{m+m+m}=2
$$
so coordinates of $\mathrm{C} . \mathrm{M}$. of three particle are (2,2)
$\mathrm{V}=300 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

solution.text: $x_{1}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}, x_{2}=\mathrm{L}, x_{3}=\frac{5 \mathrm{~L}}{4}$ $\therefore x_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{m_{1} x_{1}+m_{2} x_{2}+m_{3} x_{3}}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}$ $=\frac{\mathrm{M} \times \frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}+\mathrm{M} \times \mathrm{L}+\mathrm{M} \times \frac{5 \mathrm{~L}}{4}}{\mathrm{M}+\mathrm{M}+\mathrm{M}}=\frac{11 \mathrm{~L}}{12}$

question.text: A trolley having mass of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>200</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> moves with uniform speed of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>36</mn><mo> </mo><msup><mi>kmh</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> on a frictionless track. A child of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>20</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> runs on the trolley from one end to the other (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> away)  with a speed of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> relative to the trolley in a direction opposite to its inotion and ultimately jumps out of the trolley. With how much velocity has the trolley moved from the time the child begins to run?

solution.text:
since, no external force is acting on the system, we can apply conservation of linear momentum.

Speed of 200 kg trolley =36×100060×60=10 m s-1

If u be the initial velocity of trolley, vb be the absolute velocity of the boy after the beginning of journey of the boy, their relative velocity is 4.

So, v'-vb=4⇒vb=v'-4

Now, applying law of conservation of momentum,

Momentum before the boy begins tu run
= Momentum after the beginning of boy's running

⇒  220×10=200v'+20v'-4

2200=220v'-80⇒220v'=2280

v'=2280220=10.36 m s-1

question.text: A ball falling freely from a height of $4.9 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, hits a horizontal surface. If $e=\frac{3}{4}$, then the ball will hit the surface, second time after

solution.text:
$\begin{aligned}
\text {Velocity on hitting the surface } & =\sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 4.9} \\
& =9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$
Velocity after first bounce, $v=\frac{3}{4} \times 9.8$

question.text: A particle of mass $m$ moving with velocity $v$ collides with a stationary particle of mass $2 \mathrm{~m}$. After collision, they stick together and continue to move together with velocity

solution.text:
Applying conservation of linear momentum
$\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_{\mathrm{i}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_{\mathrm{f}}(\because \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{mv})$
$m v_1+2 m v_2=(m+2 m) v^{\prime}$
$m v^1+2 m \times 0=(3 m) v^{\prime}$
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{mv}=3 \mathrm{mv}^{\prime} \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{v}}{3}$

question.text: Consider elastic collision of a particle of mass m moving with a velocity u with another particle of the same mass at rest. After the collision the projectile and the struck particle move in directions making angles $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ respectively with the initial direction of motion. The sum of the angles $\theta_{1}+\theta_{2},$ is :
A neutron moving with speed v makes a head on collision with a hydrogen atom in ground state kept at rest. The minimum kinetic energy of the neutron for which inelastic collision takes place is

solution.text:
Let speed of neutron before collision $=\mathrm{V}$ Speed of neutron after collision $=\mathrm{V}_{1}$ Speed of proton or hydrogen atom after collision $=\mathrm{V}_{2}$ Energy of excitation $=\Delta \mathrm{E}$ From the law of conservation of linear momentum, $\mathrm{mv}=\mathrm{mv}_{1}+\mathrm{mv}_{2}$

And for law of conservation of energy,

$$

\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}_{2}^{2}

$$

From squaring eq. (i), we get

$$

v^{2}=v_{1}^{2}+v_{2}^{2}+2 v_{1} v_{2}

$$

From squaring eq. (ii), we get

$$

v^{2}=v_{1}^{2}+v_{2}^{2}+\frac{2 \Delta E}{m}

$$

From eqn (3) \& (4)

$$

\begin{aligned}

\therefore 2 \mathrm{v}_{1} \mathrm{v}_{2} &=\frac{2 \Delta \mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{m}} \\

\therefore\left(\mathrm{v}_{1}-\mathrm{v}_{2}\right)^{2} &=\left(\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mathrm{v}_{2}\right)^{2}-4 \mathrm{v}_{1} \mathrm{v}_{2}=\mathrm{v}^{2}-\frac{4 \Delta \mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{m}}

\end{aligned}

$$

As, $v_{1}-v_{2}$ must be real, $v^{2}-\frac{4 \Delta E}{m} \geq 0$

$$

\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^{2} \geq 2 \Delta \mathrm{E}

$$

The minimum energy that can be absorbed by the hydrogen atom in the ground state to go into the excited state is $10.2 \mathrm{eV}$. Therefore, the maximum kinetic energy needed is

$$

\frac{1}{2} m v_{\min }^{2}=2 \times 10.2=20.4 \mathrm{eV}

$$

question.text: A particle of mass $10 \mathrm{~kg}$ moving eastwards with a speed $5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ collides with another particle of the same mass moving north-wards with the same speed $5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. The two particles coalesce on collision. The new particle of mass $20 \mathrm{~kg}$ will move in the north-east direction with velocity

solution.text:
Here $\hat{i} m v+\hat{j} m v=2 m \vec{V}$
That is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}(\hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}})$
Hence $V=\frac{v}{2} \times \sqrt{2}=\frac{v}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot\left[\right.$ Here $\left.v=5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}\right]$
$$
\text { So, } V=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
$$
